title: Body cam footage could overload the justice system, warns senior Crown prosecutor
summary: Body cameras can be a valuable source of evidence for the justice system, but it gives legal professionals a lot of extra footage to review. The head of the province’s Crown Attorney Association says…

blocks.text: Nfld. & Labrador·New

Body cameras can be a valuable source of evidence for the justice system, but it gives legal professionals a lot of extra footage to review. The head of the province’s Crown Attorney Association says there’s not enough resources for prosecutors to process body camera footage.
Shawn Patten, president of the N.L. Crown Attorneys Association, says prosecutors need more resources
Body-cam footage could overload the justice system, says senior crown prosecutor
Body-worn cameras provide the courts with evidence that can be valuable but a Newfoundland and Labrador Crown prosecutor says it also risks overloading an already struggling justice system.
Shawn Patten, the president of the province’s Crown Attorneys Association, says the extra evidence from RCMP body-worn cameras is taking a toll on crown prosecutors.
The Royal Newfoundland Constabulary will begin its rollout of body cameras in 2027, which means more footage will be heading to the courts. Petten said that will only add to the court’s workload.
Patten told CBC News it is “all but impossible without more resources to ensure that we can adequately review that material.”
Shawn Patten, president of the N. L. Crown Attorneys Association, says they will need more resources to handle the additional workload. (Danny Arsenault/CBC)
Budget 2026 earmarked funding for six new Crown attorneys, but Patten said numbers are stagnant and retention is a problem.
Justice minister Helen Conway Ottenheimer said in addition to more resources, there is also a “need to look at making efficiencies throughout the entire justice system.”
Last month, Conway Ottenheimer announced $900,000 has been allocated for RNC body cameras and $500,000 for the Digital Evidence Management System.
She said body cameras and the new software is a step toward modernization, which will help bring the “justice system up to par with the rest of the country, because it's been lagging in that regard."
Body cams in use at RCMP for over a year

“We want to ensure that the public has that trust in the RCMP and [using body cameras] is a big way to ensure that we continue to establish that,” says RCMP media relations officer Cpl. Jesse O’Donaghey.
RCMP media relations officer Cpl. Jesse O’Donaghey says using body cameras helps build trust between the police and community. (Danny Arsenault/CBC)
Newfoundland and Labrador RCMP has already rolled out its body-worn camera in all of its detachments since 2025, and its footage has already made its way through the courts.

In February, 2026 the Serious Incident Response Team, a civilian-led police oversight agency, cleared RCMP officers of wrongdoing after shooting a man in mental health distress after he pointed an unloaded BB gun at them.
The report on the incident cites hours of body-worn camera footage as evidence.

Another report on a separate incident involving an RCMP officer who fired his gun at a vehicle fleeing police did not cite body-worn camera footage. Stephen Ring, the author of the report, writes that although some body-cam footage was provided, none was available from officers present during the discharge of the weapon.
The officers involved were also cleared of wrongdoing.
